title_original: Sofia Bassi’s Market Is Heating Up as Female Surrealists Get Their Due
excerpt_original: Pippy Houldsworth Gallery is showing 16 of the Mexican painter’s works in London as auction prices climb.

blocks.text: Sofia Bassi ’s paintings are portals. In Eclosión (1969), an eye formed of sinew and vapor bursts out of an egg, a whirling gyre reigns over ruined buildings, and a pair of skeletons make an inspection. Devise your own narrative. It’s an absurd and unsettling dreamscape, something Hieronymus Bosch might have painted in a furious mood.

Eclosión is one of 16 works by the Mexican Surrealist on display at Pippy Houldsworth Gallery , which is mounting the artist’s first European solo exhibition, “Floating Between Earth and Sky,” through November 14. The show arrives as demand for Bassi’s work reaches new highs at auction.

“There has been a surge of interest in female Surrealists.” Pippy Houldsworth said in an email. “ Leonora Carrington and Remedios Varo have become household names, both of whom Bassi associated with. Despite this, Bassi has remained largely unknown outside of Mexico. Her work more than holds up to her contemporaries.”
To further Bassi’s exposure, the gallery is also including Untitled (1969), a round landscape with Surrealist symbols, at its booth at Frieze London. The work is priced at $85,000.

Bassi, who died in 1998, at 85, only picked up the brush in her 50s. Her oeuvre grew darker between 1968 and 1972, when she was imprisoned in Acapulco after pleading guilty to the murder of her son-in-law. ( Eclosión is signed “ELC”, an abbreviation of “En la Cárcel,” Spanish for “in prison.”) Works from this period, priced between $20,000 and $400,000, form the focus of Houldsworth’s show.
Sofia Bassi, Untitled (1969). Photo: courtesy Prudence Cuming Associates Ltd / Pippy Houldsworth Gallery,

The gallery’s presentation is in partnership with Bassi’s Foundation, run by her daughter-in-law and granddaughter, and Georgina Pounds Gallery in Mexico City, an early booster that staged the largest exhibition dedicated to Bassi to date this past spring. While the foundation retains some of Bassi’s best paintings, many more are spread among Latin American private collections.

Pounds is clear about the impact of prison on Bassi’s career. In 1967, she was one of seven female artists exhibited alongside Frida Kahlo in a landmark exhibition at Mexico City’s Museum of Modern Art (MAM). A year later, she was behind bars.

“Imprisonment became inseparable from her public biography and to some extent overshadowed her practice,” Pounds said in an email. “Her work subsequently receded from dominant histories of Mexican modernism and Surrealism.”

That could be changing. In May, Mexico’s Morton auction house sold Bassi’s Muñeca Reina (1974), a fiery woodscape haunted by a long-necked girl, for a record 800,000 Mexican pesos ($46,000). An untitled work, from 1992, sold for $44,800 at Sotheby’s on October 9, doubling it’s high estimate.

According to the Artnet Price Database, Bassi’s works have sold for an average of $29,291 at auction so far in 2026, more than double the $12,897 average in 2025 and well above the $3,000 to $7,000 that was typical through the 2010s.

Earlier this year, the collector Christian Levett acquired four Bassi works from Georgina Pounds Gallery for his museum dedicated to female artists. Bassi’s works are also in the collections of the Tel Aviv Museum of Art and MAM. An institutional show, Pounds said, is in the offing.
